parts: Lesson 10: Securing the Computer System — Summary

Cyber security (Information Technology Security or Cyber Safety) is the processes, practices and techniques that protect devices, networks, data and programs from attack, damage or unauthorized access. Unauthorized access is a cyber crime (online transaction fraud, online stalking, identity theft, child pornography) punishable under the Indian Penal Code. Need: data is available to everyone and must be protected from unauthorized access, copying and distribution; organizational data must not leak to competitors; personal data on social media is prone to hacking; and cyber attacks and digital spying threaten national security.

Always password protect your system, applications and files: do not share passwords, do not use the same password for all applications, make it strong with alphabets, digits and special characters, do not use initials, date of birth or pet's name, keep it 8–10 characters and use a password manager. Always update the operating system, antivirus and other software (updates add features and close security loopholes). Always pay attention to security warnings. Always install original antivirus: antivirus software protects the system from viruses, worms, Trojans and other malware; it does not give 100% assurance, so use only original antivirus and update it regularly. Never open unsolicited mails or click links in them. Download authenticated, reputable software from the official site and ignore ads. Scan files before downloading. Enable the firewall: a barrier between your computer/network and the internet that blocks data communication by closing all ports; hardware firewall (built into home routers) or software firewall (built into the OS; enable through Control Panel, System and Security); antivirus often includes one. Adjust browser settings (block cookies, ads, location access; options are disabled by default; in Chrome use the Customize and Control Google Chrome button). Use anti-spy software: spyware secretly gathers information such as banking and card details and sends it to a third party. Back up your data on a secondary storage device or the cloud. Uninstall programs no longer in use (safer and faster).

Cyber law (Internet Law, IT Law, Law of the Internet) deals with legal issues of electronic devices, internet and related services: online privacy, intellectual property, freedom of expression, internet usage, online transaction frauds. Cyber crime is any unlawful act using digital devices connected to the internet: online fraud (credit card theft, identity theft), copyright infringement (unauthorized download and usage), defamation (fake public statements harming reputation), cyber stalking and cyber bullying, business ethics (trade secrets protected) and identity theft.

The IT Act 2000 (based on the Indian Penal Code 1860, Indian Evidence Act 1872, Bankers' Books Evidence Act 1891 and RBI Act 1934) is the primary law for cyber crime and e-commerce in India. Salient features: legal recognition of electronic transactions and of digital signatures; facilitates online correspondence with government (file returns, pay taxes, apply for passports and Aadhaar); allows electronic storage of data; allows online money transfer; defines offences, penalties and breaches; lays down trial procedure; penalties for damaging computer systems and cyber terrorism; Section 66A made offensive messages illegal. Report a cyber crime to the cyber cell of the local police station or online at the cyber crime portal (cybercrime.gov.in), where anonymous complaints are possible. Advantages: addresses security of data and services; encourages healthy trade practices under legal provisions; digital signatures make exchange of authenticated documents easy; improves e-governance.

E-waste (electronic waste) is old electric or electronic devices no longer in use (computers, laptops, mobiles, tablets). In a landfill it leaches toxic chemicals which contaminate groundwater and drinking water. Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment (WEEE) is a major threat. Harmful effects: lead (monitors, batteries) causes lead poisoning, harming brain development, the central nervous system and kidneys; mercury causes respiratory disorders and brain damage; plastics damage the immune system and cause stress and anxiety; burning motherboards produces beryllium, which causes lung cancer, skin diseases and allergies; cadmium is also toxic. Efficient disposal is e-waste management; the most feasible methods are recycling (e-waste converted into reusable material; dismantle to extract copper, gold; wear gloves and masks), refurbishing (renovating and selling again at lower prices) and re-use (using a device again after slight modification). The government should set up recycling units, arrange safe storage, encourage research, enforce strict laws and punish open burning, acid baths and landfill dumping. More than 55 million tonnes of e-waste is generated globally every year.
